# Exercises {#sec-m1-exercicios}

Do the exercises **before** opening the solutions. They all use the coastal shipping dataset prepared
below; some ask you to go back to the raw file on purpose.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(readxl)

colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-"))
names(cabotagem) <- colunas

cabotagem <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |>
  dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(uf_origem  = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem),
         uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino),
         tku_bi     = tku / 1e9)

nrow(cabotagem)
```

## 1. Types and inspection

Find out, without looking at the answer: how many text columns and how many numeric columns does the dataset have?
Which commodity (`sh2`) has the largest number of records?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
table(sapply(cabotagem, class))

cabotagem |> dplyr::count(sh2, sort = TRUE) |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 3)
```
:::

## 2. Combined filters

How many links have their destination in the Northeast region **and** the profile "Carga Conteinerizada"
(container cargo)? What is the total TKU of these links?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
nordeste <- c("AL","BA","CE","MA","PB","PE","PI","RN","SE")

cabotagem |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_destino %in% nordeste, perfil == "Carga Conteinerizada") |>
  dplyr::summarise(ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = round(sum(tku_bi), 2))
```
:::

## 3. Text

Create a `capitulo_sh` column with only the HS chapter code (the characters before the
hyphen in `sh2`) and count how many distinct chapters there are. Then list the five
chapters with the highest TKU, with the readable description.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    capitulo_sh = stringr::str_extract(sh2, "^[^-]+"),
    descricao   = stringr::str_remove(sh2, "^[^-]+-") |> stringr::str_squish()
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(capitulo_sh, descricao)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |>
  dplyr::mutate(descricao = stringr::str_trunc(descricao, 45), tku_bi = round(tku_bi, 1))
```
:::

## 4. Dates

Each module's asynchronous material is released the day after the second session. Given the
vector with the dates of the second sessions of Option A, compute each module's release date
and the corresponding day of the week. How many days are there between the first and the last release?

```{r}
segundos_encontros <- as.Date(c("2026-09-30", "2026-10-07", "2026-10-14",
                                "2026-10-21", "2026-11-04"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
library(lubridate)

liberacao <- segundos_encontros + lubridate::days(1)

data.frame(
  modulo = 1:5,
  encontro = format(segundos_encontros, "%d/%m/%Y"),
  liberacao = format(liberacao, "%d/%m/%Y"),
  dia_semana = lubridate::wday(liberacao, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
)

as.numeric(max(liberacao) - min(liberacao))
```
:::

## 5. Grouping and shares

For each cargo profile, which destination state is the most important and what percentage of the profile's
TKU does it represent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(perfil, uf_destino)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = tku_bi / sum(tku_bi), .by = perfil) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(tku_bi, n = 1, by = perfil) |>
  dplyr::transmute(perfil, uf_destino,
            tku_bi = round(tku_bi, 1),
            part = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))
```
:::

## 6. *Long* → *wide*

Build a table with one row per destination state and one column per cargo profile, containing the
TKU in billions, with a final total column, ordered by the total. Zeros where there is no flow.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(uf_destino, perfil)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = perfil, values_from = tku_bi, values_fill = 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(total = rowSums(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric)))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
:::

## 7. A `join` with a diagnosis

The table below has the estimated population of some port municipalities. Join it with the TKU
attracted by destination municipality and answer: which municipalities in the coastal shipping dataset are **not**
in the population table? What is the TKU per inhabitant of those that matched?

```{r}
populacao <- data.frame(
  municipio = c("Santos", "Paranaguá", "Itajaí", "São Luís", "Manaus",
                "Rio de Janeiro", "Salvador", "Suape", "Angra dos Reis"),
  pop = c(418375, 156174, 223112, 1037775, 2063547, 6211223, 2417678, NA, 182000)
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
por_municipio <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(cidade_destino, uf_destino)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))

# diagnosis: what does not match (top 10 by TKU)
por_municipio |>
  dplyr::anti_join(populacao, by = c("cidade_destino" = "municipio")) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10)

# the join, taking care not to lose rows
resultado <- por_municipio |>
  dplyr::left_join(populacao, by = c("cidade_destino" = "municipio"),
            relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(pop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(tku_por_hab = tku_bi * 1e9 / pop) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_por_hab))

resultado |>
  dplyr::transmute(cidade_destino, uf_destino,
            tku_bi = round(tku_bi, 1),
            pop,
            `t·km per inhabitant` = scales::comma(round(tku_por_hab)))
```

Note that most destination municipalities are **not** in the population table: in
real work, that table would come from `censobr`/`sidrar` with the IBGE code as the key, not from
a typed-in list. That is exactly the subject of modules 2 and 3.
:::

## 8. A complete chart

Reproduce a horizontal bar chart with the 12 largest destination port facilities
by TKU, with value labels, a formatted axis, title, subtitle
and source.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-instalacoes
#| fig-cap: "Twelve largest destination facilities by coastal shipping TKU"
#| fig-height: 5.5
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(instalacao_destino, uf_destino)) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(tku_bi, n = 12) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rotulo = stringr::str_c(stringr::str_trunc(instalacao_destino, 28), " (", uf_destino, ")")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(rotulo, tku_bi))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::number(tku_bi, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ","),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Coastal shipping: destination facilities by TKU",
    subtitle = "Billions of tonne-kilometres, 2025",
    x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: ANTAQ, Estatístico Aquaviário (TB6.1)."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::

## 9. Challenge: a reusable function

Write a function `resumir_por(dados, coluna)` that takes the dataset and the **name of a column**
and returns the total TKU, the number of links and the percentage share for each category of that
column, sorted. Test it with `perfil`, `uf_destino` and `sh2`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
resumir_por <- function(dados, coluna) {
  dados |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      ligacoes = dplyr::n(),
      tku_bi   = sum(tku_bi),
      .by = {{ coluna }}
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(part = tku_bi / sum(tku_bi)) |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(tku_bi = round(tku_bi, 2),
           part   = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1))
}

resumir_por(cabotagem, perfil)
resumir_por(cabotagem, uf_destino) |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 5)
```

The `{{ coluna }}` (called *embrace*) is `dplyr`'s mechanism for writing functions that
take unquoted column names. It is what turns an analysis into a reusable
tool. It will be used in module 5 to produce one report per municipality from a
single template.
:::
